say.text: A question bank from an old year gives three lines. Which one still holds for a 2026 paper?

choices.label: Carcinoma cervix is the commonest cancer in Indian women
Carcinoma breast is the commonest cancer in Indian women
FNAC is the investigation of choice for a breast lump
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Breast cancer has overtaken cervix as the most common cancer in women in India and worldwide.
Ask which of the three answers newer evidence and newer guidelines have overtaken, and which one they have not.
That choice is not right. Cervix was the textbook answer for years, so it feels like a safe fact to copy.
Ask whether the epidemiology has moved since that key was written.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the key first: old papers expected cervix, and current teaching has moved on.

say.text: That choice is not right. Many old papers did expect FNAC for a lump, so the line feels familiar.
Ask what the sample must report before the team can plan treatment.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the key: old papers asked for FNAC, but current practice asks which sample gives receptor status.

say.text: A 50-year-old has a palpable breast mass. Before neoadjuvant chemotherapy starts, the team needs the tumour type and receptor status. Which sample do you request?

choices.label: Fine needle aspiration of the breast mass
Core needle biopsy of the breast mass
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A core sample shows invasion and grade, and it gives ER, PR and HER2 status, which the plan needs.
Ask whether a few stray cells can tell the team the tumour's type and its receptor status.
That choice is not right. Fine needle aspiration is quick and cheap, and old keys taught it as the breast test.
Ask whether cells alone can report invasion and receptor status, or whether a piece of tissue is needed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the reason: invasion and receptor status come from tissue, not from cells alone.

say.text: A 2.5 cm tumour has orange-peel skin over it and a small ulcer nearby. There is no redness or warmth. What is the T category?

choices.label: T4d, for inflammatory carcinoma of the breast
T4b, for skin ulceration and peau d'orange
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Ulceration and orange-peel skin are skin involvement, so T4b; T4d needs the red, warm, swollen breast.
Ask which T4 category needs the whole inflammatory picture, with redness and warmth, and which needs only a skin finding.
That choice is not right. Orange-peel skin is the sign people tie to inflammatory cancer, so T4d comes to mind first.
Ask whether the breast is red, warm and swollen, or whether the skin shows a single sign.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the sign: a skin change is not the whole inflammatory picture.

say.text: A woman has a 2 cm invasive cancer and a hard node above the collarbone on the same side. Chest X-ray and bone scan are clear. What is her M category?

choices.label: M1; a node beyond the axilla is distant
M0; the same-side node is nodal, N3c
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Same-side supraclavicular nodes are N3c on the nodal ladder, and M1 needs distant organ spread.
Ask whether a node on the same side is a distant site, or a further station on the nodal ladder.
That choice is not right. A node above the clavicle looks far from the breast, so it feels like spread beyond it.
Ask which letter of the staging system a node belongs to, and which letter is for distant sites.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the classification: older keys counted these nodes differently from current staging.

say.text: A classmate writes: 'Halsted radical mastectomy is the standard operation for operable carcinoma breast.' Which correction do you write?

choices.label: Halsted stays standard, as the most definitive operation
Conservation with radiotherapy, or MRM, by suitability
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Operable cancer is now treated with breast conservation and radiotherapy, or MRM; Halsted is rarely done.
Ask what the newer operations keep, and whether the most extensive operation is still chosen by default.
That choice is not right. Halsted is the textbook definitive operation, so the classmate's line sounds familiar.
Ask whether removing more muscle is what decides the operation now, or whether suitability does.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the key: old papers expected Halsted; check what current practice has moved to.

say.text: A classmate marks a tumour T4a because it is fixed to pectoralis major. Ribs, intercostals and serratus are free. What is the correction?

choices.label: Not T4a; pectoralis fixity alone is not chest wall
T4a stands; fixity to pectoralis is chest-wall disease
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. T4a chest-wall invasion means ribs, intercostals or serratus anterior; the pectoralis major is not on that list.
Ask which structures the T4a list names, and whether the pectoralis is one of them.
That choice is not right. Muscle fixity feels like deep invasion, so the pectoralis gets counted as chest wall.
Ask which tissues the T4a chest-wall list names.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the list: the fixity test is a test of fixity, and the T4a list names other tissues.

say.text: Your patient on trastuzumab has a falling ejection fraction. What do you expect when the drug is held?

choices.label: Permanent damage that grows with dose, like doxorubicin
Often recovers after the drug is held
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is usually reversible and not dose-related, unlike the anthracycline pattern.
Ask whether a HER2 antibody injures the heart the same way an anthracycline does.
That choice is not right. Doxorubicin is the cardiotoxic drug most students remember, so its pattern gets carried across.
Ask which drug the cumulative-dose pattern belongs to, and whether a HER2 antibody follows it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the drug class: the cumulative, largely irreversible pattern belongs to anthracyclines.

say.text: A 36-year-old woman has an ER-positive early cancer and has not reached menopause. Which hormonal drug fits her?

choices.label: Anastrozole, since her tumour is ER-positive
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Before menopause the ovaries supply most oestrogen, so tamoxifen blocks the receptor; aromatase inhibitors suit postmenopausal women.
Ask where this woman's oestrogen comes from, and whether her ovaries still make it.
That choice is not right. ER positivity is the cue most people act on, so the drug follows the receptor alone.
Ask whether menopausal status changes where the oestrogen comes from.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check her status: aromatase inhibitors act on oestrogen made by peripheral aromatisation after menopause.

say.text: Your patient on tamoxifen asks what it does to her womb. Which answer is right?

choices.label: Endometrial atrophy, which protects against cancer
Endometrial carcinoma is a recognised risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Tamoxifen acts differently in the endometrium, so it raises endometrial cancer risk, and it also carries thromboembolism risk.
Ask whether a drug that blocks oestrogen in the breast blocks it in every tissue.
That choice is not right. Tamoxifen's anti-oestrogen effect in the breast is the part most learners remember, so the uterus gets assumed protected too.
Ask whether the same drug behaves the same way in every tissue.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the tissue: tamoxifen is not a pure blocker in the uterus, and its uterine effect is a known adverse effect.

say.text: A core biopsy of a mammographic area shows classic LCIS, with no invasive cancer. What is the plan?

choices.label: Mastectomy on that side, to remove the lesion
Surveillance, and chemoprevention may be considered
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Classic LCIS marks a raised risk of invasive cancer in either breast, so it is watched, and chemoprevention is considered.
Ask whether classic LCIS is a cancer to be removed, or a marker of future risk.
That choice is not right. Carcinoma in situ sounds like cancer to be cut out, so surgery feels like the default.
Ask what this lesion predicts, not only what it looks like on the biopsy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the lesion: classic LCIS is a risk marker, not an invasive cancer.

say.text: An MRI shows multicentric disease in both breasts. Which type of breast carcinoma is most often bilateral and multicentric?

choices.label: Invasive ductal carcinoma, the commonest type
Invasive lobular carcinoma, the typical bilateral type
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Lobular carcinoma loses E-cadherin, so cells grow in single file and it is more often bilateral and multicentric.
Ask which type the question's bilateral cue points to, not which type is most frequent.
That choice is not right. Ductal carcinoma is the commonest type, so it feels like the answer to any type question.
Ask which histology the bilateral and multicentric pattern points to, not which is most frequent.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the pattern: frequency and bilateral spread are different questions.

say.text: Which pairing of gene, chromosome arm and male breast cancer is right?

choices.label: BRCA2 on 17q, linked to male breast cancer
BRCA1 on 17q, linked to male breast cancer
BRCA2 on 13q, linked to male breast cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. BRCA2 lies on 13q and is the gene more linked to male breast cancer; BRCA1, on 17q, tends to give triple-negative tumours.
Ask which gene is linked to male breast cancer first, then the arm that gene sits on.
That choice is not right. The numbers 13 and 17 are easy to swap, so the arm slips onto the wrong gene.
Ask which arm BRCA1 sits on, then which arm is left for BRCA2.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the arms: the two numbers belong to different genes.

say.text: That choice is not right. BRCA1 is the best-known breast cancer gene, so it gets attached to every phenotype.
Ask which gene the male phenotype belongs to, before you name the arm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the phenotype: the male-linked gene is the one the question names, and it is not BRCA1.

say.text: Your classmate writes 'carcinoma is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge'. What do you write for the most common cause?

choices.label: Intraductal papilloma, a benign duct lesion
Carcinoma breast, the most worrying cause
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause; carcinoma must still be excluded when the discharge is bloody.
Ask which question is being answered: the most common cause, or the cause that must be excluded.
That choice is not right. Blood in the discharge is the alarm sign, so danger seems to decide the frequency too.
Ask which question the classmate answered: the most common cause, or the cause to rule out.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two questions: frequency and alarm are different.
